title: Te Papa

paragraphs.text: Located in the capital city, Wellington, the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa is the national museum and art gallery of New Zealand. It is commonly known as ‘Te Papa’, its Maori* name, which can be translated to mean ‘container of treasures’. Inside the building are six floors of exhibitions, cafés and gift shops dedicated to New Zealand’s people and environment. The museum also incorporates outdoor areas with artificial caves, native bushes and wetlands.

Building Te Papa was an engineering feat. Jasmax Architects won an international competition to design Te Papa, and their brief was to create a building that reflected the country’s evolving identity. The site was previously occupied by a modern five-storey hotel, which was taken off its foundations and transported along eight sets of parallel rails to a new site 200 metres down the road, where it is now known as the Museum Art Hotel.

The museum took four years to complete and weighs 64,000 tonnes, including 80,000 cubic metres of concrete. It has 36,000 square metres of public floor space, and is clad in 14,500 grey and yellow stone panels. The building sits on 150 shock absorbers to protect it from earthquake movement, and care has been taken to use local materials in the construction. For instance, the wood used inside for the panels, ceilings and handrails is from native New Zealand trees.

Te Papa’s north face faces Wellington’s harbour. Its cliff-like walls embrace nature —the sea, hills, and sky. Here sits the Marae (the Maori communal meeting place) which welcomes visitors from New Zealand and around the world, and leads them to the Maori exhibition areas. Te Papa’s south face, with its vibrantly coloured panels, looks out towards the city. The southern area inside the museum is oriented towards exhibitions with a pakeha (European) focus. Its spaces resemble a grid, reflecting the patterns of the European settlement of New Zealand. The central hall is a wedge that divides, but also unites Te Papa’s north and south faces, which can be seen to represent the natural and the urban, the Maori and the European. Here in this central wedge, an exhibition explores the Treaty of Waitangi —the nation’s founding document. Here too is the Community Gallery, which houses temporary exhibitions from specific communities that have settled in New Zealand, for example, Chinese, Dutch and Indian.

The idea of gateways is particularly meaningful at Te Papa. Two important waharoa (the Maori term for gateways) are on display—a contemporary one on the Marae and a traditional one in the foyer on the second floor. The entire museum is also intended to be a ‘gateway’ to New Zealand’s natural and cultural heritage.

The three large stones by Te Papa’s main entrance symbolise the museum’s commitment to New Zealand’s land and people. Specifically, the middle stone represents Papatuanuku, the Earth Mother; the stone nearest the street represents the Maori, the indigenous people of New Zealand; the stone nearest the entrance represents the Tangata Tiriti, the people who settled in New Zealand and were given land rights according to the Treaty of Waitangi. The first two stones are lava that erupted from Mount Taranaki about 75,000 years ago. The third stone is Karamea granite, a stone that is a symbol of permanence. This granite is about 350 million years old and comes from the Oparara River, north of Karamea on the West Coast of the South Island of New Zealand. Its various colours reflect the diversity of those who came to settle in New Zealand.

There is also a large ball inside Te Papa’s main entrance, called the Sponsorship Recognition Stone. It acknowledges the founding sponsors who contributed to the building of Te Papa. Low-pressure water from a 500-litre tank provides the power to rotate the ball. The layer of water between the ball and base is just 0.2 millimetres thick and visitors can push the ball to turn it on its base. Jets pulse the water to keep the ball moving when no one is pushing it and, for hygiene reasons, the water is treated with swimming-pool chemicals and changed weekly. The stone is 1.4 billion years old—the oldest material in Te Papa. It is a coarse crystalline basalt from Transvaal, South Africa, weighing 0.79 tonnes and measuring 82 centimetres in diameter.

In terms of Te Papa’s strategic priorities, the museum’s management states them as follows: ‘As a cultural and intellectual leader, Te Papa will signpost pathways to the future by initiating, hosting and engaging in debates that explore a wide range of contemporary issues. Te Papa will engage and excite by conducting leading edge research, and by communicating and modelling environmentally responsible practices that are smart, accessible, and inspiring.’
